summary:
## Verdict

Critical CORS regression: this change turns a single-origin allowlist into a reflect-any-origin policy while still advertising credentialed access.

## Analysis

`corsHeaders` previously returned `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` + `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` only when `origin` was in `ALLOWED` (`https://app.example.com`). The new path always returns:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <request Origin>` (or `*` when `origin` is null)
- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`

Any malicious site can therefore make a credentialed cross-origin request and read the response in a supporting browser. That is a full break of the prior same-origin credential boundary.

The stated rationale (native mobile / arbitrary webview origins) does not justify this. CORS is enforced by browsers; native HTTP clients are not subject to it. Mobile webviews still send a concrete Origin and should be allowlisted (or use a separate non-cookie auth path), not mirrored unconditionally.

Secondary issue on the null-origin branch: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is invalid per the Fetch CORS algorithm; browsers ignore that pair. The dangerous case is the non-null branch that echoes the attacker Origin.

## Recommendation

Restore an explicit allowlist (extend it with known webview/app origins if needed). Never pair `credentials: true` with `*` or with an unchecked reflected Origin.

**Recommendation:** request-changes
